title: Not ten thousand years
hookLine: don't act as if you'll live ten thousand years; while you can, be good (Meditations 4.17)

cards: Ten thousand years. That's the number Marcus Aurelius chose, and it's meant to be absurd. Nobody plans on living that long.

And yet a thank-you waits a season, then a year. An apology stays ready in the head and never reaches the mouth. A visit to an aunt who keeps saying come anytime slides to some later month, as though later were endless.
In book four Marcus wrote himself a reminder short enough for a sticky note. Today: not ten thousand years.

teach.h: A WARNING, A FACT, AN INSTRUCTION.
teach.b: In George Long's 1862 translation, the seventeenth entry reads: "Do not act as if thou wert going to live ten thousand years. Death hangs over thee. While thou livest, while it is in thy power, be good."
A warning, a fact, and an instruction. Ten thousand years is the joke inside the warning.
Marcus isn't accusing himself of a belief. He's accusing himself of a habit: putting off the good because there always seems to be more time. Death hangs over you.
He doesn't say it to frighten himself.

teach.h: DEATH IN VIEW, TO SORT WHAT MATTERS.
teach.b: Stoic writers kept death in view on purpose, as a way of sorting what matters from what doesn't. If this might be the last week, the thank-you note moves up, and the argument about the thermostat moves down.
Then: while you can, be good. Notice he doesn't say be productive, or be well-known, or finish your list. He says be good.

teach.h: WHILE IT IS IN YOUR POWER.
teach.b: And he puts a condition on it: while it is in your power. Not when you're less busy. Not when the kids are grown.
Not when you've earned a rest.
The good you've been saving isn't kept somewhere safe. It's quietly expiring. Is later actually promised?
Marcus's answer, in three short sentences, was no.

how: Some readers of Marcus Aurelius use Meditations 4.17 as a prompt to stop postponing small kindnesses.

mention it if you ever run into them.

practice: Let the number ten thousand sit there for a moment, and smile at it if you like, then come back to this one hour. Who will you see in it: a coworker, a child, a stranger at the counter, a voice on the phone?
Choose one, and ask quietly what being good to them would look like: a real thank-you, full attention, a patient answer.

wordCard.voice: George Long, whose 1862 translation renders Marcus's warning: do not act as if you had ten thousand years, but be good while it's in your power. Today's word.

orig.note: Greek, 'good': Marcus's instruction in 4.17 is simply to become good while you can.

carryVoice: Your line: be good while I can. While it is in my power, not someday. Until tomorrow.
